paper_title: How Much Training-Inference Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without requiring a full training run for each candidate. Model-specific FP8 recipes preserve training quality while providing capacity for at least $1.93\times$ as many KV-cache tokens as BF16. Combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same training quality $1.62\times$ sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Code is available at https://github.com/benyucong/train-inference-mismatch-opd

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains student model on responses it samples itself, guided by fixed teacher that scores every token (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). It brings stronger or specialized teachers ability into the student, and many recent model releases run it as post-training stage (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; NVIDIA et al., 2026). Its cost lies in producing the responses, called rollouts, which can dominate training time (Kang et al., 2026; Qiu et al., 2026). With standard inference engine in 16-bit BF16, rollout generation and teacher scoring take 76% of each training steps time on the 7B student (App. Table 10). Therefore, cheaper rollouts mean cheaper OPD. Two techniques make rollouts cheaper. Quantized inference stores the rollout engines weights and key-value (KV) cache in fewer bits, such as the 8-bit FP8 format, so the same GPUs hold more rollouts (Qiu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025b). Asynchronous rollouts let generation run ahead of training, so the trainer does not wait for it, and the rollouts come from weights few versions old (Fu et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026). However, both come at price: the rollout engine that generates the rollouts no longer runs exactly the model being trained, so the student learns from responses that are not quite its own. We call this gap mismatch and measure it as the per-token KL divergence between the two models next-token distributions, in nats per token. Even standard engine has small mismatch, because inference engines and trainers use different kernels and numerics (Liu et al., 2025a; He & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), and quantization and stale weights widen it further. RL post-training can face the same traininginference mismatch. It also trains model on its own rollouts, and the mismatch can collapse training (Zhong et al., 2026). Many RL systems therefore correct the update per token (Yao et al., 2025a; Marek & Ryabinin, 2026b). Recent OPD pipelines often apply these remedies (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; NVIDIA et al., 2026). However, OPD appears far less sensitive to mismatch than RL. Semi-OPD (Zhao et al., 2026) and Lightning OPD (Wu How Much Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate? and develop lightweight admission check to evaluate new configurations without full training runs (3). Using controlled rollout configurations and evaluation criteria (4), we characterize OPDs mismatch tolerance across student models, validate the admission check, and quantify the efficiency gains of cheaper rollouts (5). Finally, we investigate why OPD behaves differently from RL under mismatch and analyze the errors that per-token corrections may miss (6). The study covers three studentteacher pairs from two model families, with 1.5B, 3B and 7B students. Each student is distilled for 200 steps from an RL-fine-tuned version of itself. On the 7B pair, we train 17 rollout configurations (4.2): six quantized ones from three production recipes, five with different degrees of asynchrony, four with different levels of weight noise, and two combining quantization with asynchrony; the 1.5B and 3B pairs add three and two FP8 runs. Our contributions are as follows: methodology for quantifying OPDs mismatch budget (3.1, 3.2, 5.1, 5.2). We define common mismatch measure and procedure for finding OPDs mismatch budget. On the 7B student, OPD preserves training quality at over 200 times the standard engines mismatch and fails at about twice that level; under the same engines, two RL methods break at about 12 and 60 times. Both mismatch and its effects vary across students. An admission check that takes minutes (3.3, 5.3, 5.4). Decisions fixed before training matched all eight tested outcomes, five from the offline check, checking six configurations in 24 minutes on one GPU. Within the budget, FP8 KV caches provide at least 1.93 times BF16s capacity, while FP8 with asynchrony reaches synchronous trainings final held-out KL 1.62 times sooner. An analysis of OPDs tolerance and its limits (5.5 and 6). We analyze why OPD tolerates mismatch differently from RL. Mismatch perturbs every OPD update but leaves its goal of matching the teacher unchanged. Its impact grows late in training, and runs beyond the observed budget fail. Under configurations OPD tolerates, uncorrected RL breaks in five of six runs. Per-token corrections can prevent these RL failures but do not improve OPD: the prefix-shift error they cannot address grows 5.3 times from passing to failing noise level, versus 2.1 times for per-token error.

sections.title: 2 BACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION
sections.content: On-policy post-training. RL post-training and OPD are both on-policy: the model learns from responses it samples itself, and both use the same update. The model pθ samples response to prompt. Each token yt follows partial response y<t, its prefix, and receives score At, its advantage. The update (cid:80) At θ log pθ(yt y<t) raises the probability of tokens with positive advantage and lowers Figure 1. OPD tolerates the mismatch of quantized rollouts, up to limit. Training accuracy (the fraction of the rollout engines responses whose final answer is correct, smoothed over 21 steps) for OPD on the 7B student, one training run per line. et al., 2026) generate rollouts once, from the untrained student, and distill on them throughout training, so the student drifts away from the rollouts. They still match or beat OPD with fresh rollouts in many settings. AsyncOPD (Kang et al., 2026) lets generation run many batches ahead of training and still reaches the accuracy of synchronous training. We call this tolerance the mismatch budget: the mismatch OPD can absorb without hurting training, which quantized and asynchronous rollouts can spend on memory and speed. We judge training by held-out KL, the students per-token KL to the teacher on held-out problems (3.2), with accuracy as second check. Figure 1 shows training accuracy on 7B student. Inside the budget, FP8 rollouts that keep the first and last layers in BF16 track the standard engine step for step, and rollouts up to 4 versions old train as well as it and finish up to 1.6 times sooner (5.4). Beyond it, every-layer FP8 rollouts are rarely correct and training fails (5.1). Whether an engine is safe is decided by the budget, not by its bit width (5.3): on this student, only quantized engines that keep the first layers KV cache in BF16 stay inside the budget. Measuring this budget and leveraging it is challenging for three reasons. (1) Different sources of mismatch are hard to compare. Quantization is set in bits and asynchrony in versions, and prior OPD studies keep the engine fixed or study staleness alone (Zhao et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a), so no common scale relates the two. (2) Checking an engine costs training run. run takes 5.5 to 6 hours on eight GPUs (5.3), too long to try engines one by one; useful check should take minutes. (3) Corrections inherited from RL may miss the damage. They act only on the error at each sampled token. Whether that is where mismatch hurts OPD, and whether these corrections widen the budget, has not been tested. We address these challenges through measurement study. First, we establish common mismatch measure to compare different rollout engines, define the mismatch budget, How Much Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate? it for those with negative one, so the advantage decides what the model learns. The two methods differ only in where the advantage comes from. In RL (Williams, 1992; Schulman et al., 2017; Ahmadian et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025), it comes from reward on the whole response, such as whether its final answer is correct, so every token of response shares one score. OPD (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025) instead lets fixed teacher pT score every token: At = log pT (yt y<t) log pθ(yt y<t), (1) which is positive when the teacher finds the token likelier than the student does. Figure 2 shows one training step. This difference decides where the update vanishes. In RL, correct response keeps its reward no matter how good the model already is, so each update pushes up the correct responses it sampled. These pushes cancel on average only if responses are sampled exactly as the model would sample them (Williams, 1992); otherwise they leave net push. In OPD, the advantage is zero at every token once the student matches the teacher, so the update vanishes there, whichever responses it trains on. Before that point, averaged over the students own samples, the update lowers KL(pθ pT ). Rollouts and mismatch. Rollout generation is major cost of on-policy training (Kang et al., 2026; Qiu et al., 2026), so systems use rollout engine such as vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). Even with synchronized weights, the engine and trainer can produce slightly different probabilities due to different kernels and numerics (Liu et al., 2025a; He & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Two speedups widen this mismatch. (i) Quantization stores engine weights or KV cache in 8 or 4 bits to fit more responses in memory, while rounding further shifts probabilities (Liu et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2026). (ii) Asynchrony overlaps generation and training, so the engine uses weights one or more updates old (Fu et al., 2025; Rang et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026). Traininginference mismatch also affects RL post-training, where its consequences are better understood. In RL, this mismatch can break training. RLs update is unbiased only over the models own samples, so the engines samples skew it regardless of reward. Each weight sync copies this drift back into the engine, where it can accumulate (Marek & Ryabinin, 2026b). Even standard vLLM engines small mismatch can make RL training fail, while an exactly matched engine does not (Zhong et al., 2026). Handling mismatch in RL. RL handles mismatch mainly in two ways. Exact matching gives the engine and trainer shared kernels or single implementation (He & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025; Wasti et al., 2025; RadixArk, 2025). It must be rebuilt for each model and GPU type and cannot Figure 2. OPD workflow and mismatch budgets. Top: 1 the rollout engine generates responses; 2 the teacher scores sampled tokens; 3 the trainer computes advantages and updates the student; and 4 updated weights are synchronized to the engine. Training runs locate the mismatch budget (5.1); each dot represents passing (blue) or failing (red) run. Bottom: the admission check estimates new engines mismatch before training (3.3). remove mismatch from quantization with BF16 trainer or asynchrony. Per-token correction keeps the mismatch and adjusts each sampled tokens update: truncated importance sampling reweights it by capped probability ratio (Yao et al., 2025a;b), token masks drop it (Ling Team et al., 2025), and score centering removes the drift (Marek & Ryabinin, 2026b). These corrections act on sampled tokens, not on which prefixes the engine reaches; for long responses, they cannot bound the error (Li et al., 2025a). Motivation: mismatch budgets in OPD. OPD pipelines use these corrections as well (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; NVIDIA et al., 2026), but mismatch may affect OPD differently because its update differs from RLs. As shown above, matching the teacher remains stationary point whichever engine generates the responses. Mismatch can still change the path to this point and degrade training quality. This raises three questions: (i) How much mismatch can OPD tolerate across different rollout engines and student models? (ii) Can we identify safe rollout configurations before training and use them to reduce rollout costs? (iii) How does mismatch affect OPDs updates, and can per-token corrections mitigate its effects? We address these questions by defining common mismatch measure, an empirical mismatch budget, and lightweight admission check (3). Using controlled rollout configurations and evaluation criteria (4), we measure tolerance, test the admission check, quantify the benefits of cheaper rollouts, and compare OPD with RL (5). Finally, we analyze update bias and the limits of per-token corrections (6). How Much Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate?

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Building on the mismatch measure, empirical budget, and admission check introduced in 3, we detail the experimental setup used to evaluate them. We describe the student teacher pairs, rollout configurations spanning quantization, stale weights, and controlled noise, and the evaluation protocols. We report the results on mismatch tolerance, admission accuracy, and rollout efficiency in 5. 4.1 Training Setup Models. We consider three student models from two model families, with sizes ranging from 1.5B to 7B parameters. The students are DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (Guo et al., 2025), and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024). Their respective teachers are Skywork-OR1-Math-7B (He et al., 2025b), JustRL-DeepSeek-1.5B (He et al., 2025a), and GTLlama-3.2-3B-Instruct-MATH. Testbed. Our testbed consists of two nodes, each equipped with four NVIDIA GH200 GPUs. In synchronous runs, one node hosts the teacher, while the other hosts the trainer and four rollout replicas. Asynchronous runs use the same eight GPUs with different placements (App. C.5). Implementation. We use vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) as the rollout engine and verl (Sheng et al., 2025) for OPD training. Unless stated otherwise, we use neither importance correction nor score centering; both are evaluated in 6. Training recipe. Each step samples 8 responses per problem for 8 DAPO-Math-17k problems (Yu et al., 2025) at temperature 1, with up to 16,384 tokens per response. The trainer takes one AdamW update per step at learning rate 106. Each budget run lasts 200 steps. 4.2 Rollout Configurations On the 7B student, we study OPDs tolerance to mismatch introduced by practical rollout optimizations (quantization and asynchrony), alone and combined. We also use weight noise to vary mismatch in controlled manner. For quantized and noisy configurations, we modify only the rollout engine; the trainer, teacher, and checkpoints remain in BF16. (i) Quantization. We test three recipes: (a) NVIDIA Model Optimizer FP8 (NVIDIA, 2026), which quantizes weights, activations, and KV cache; (b) NVFP4 (Alvarez et al., 2025), which uses 4-bit weights and activations with FP8 KV cache; and (c) vLLMs FP8 KV cache, which leaves weights and activations in BF16. We test each recipe across all layers and with variant retaining the first layers KV cache in BF16. For Model Optimizer FP8, this variant instead retains the entire first and last layers in BF16. Because NVFP4 requires Blackwell GPUs, we emulate its quantization in BF16 and evaluate quality only, not speed (App. C). (ii) Stale weights. We vary weight staleness by allowing the rollout engine to use weights up to {1, 2, 4, 8} model versions old, using verls fully asynchronous mode (meituansearch, 2026). We also test colocated generation and training, where rollouts are at most two versions old (App. C.5). (iii) Weight noise. After each weight synchronization, we add fixed Gaussian offset to the rollout engines weights, scaled by σ {0.0665, 0.15, 0.234, 0.325} times each projection matrixs standard deviation. This provides controlled perturbations along fixed weight-space direction. (iv) Combined configurations. We combine Model Optimizer FP8, retaining the first and last layers in BF16, with rollout weights up to four or eight versions old. 4.3 Evaluation and Admission Protocol We specify how we evaluate training quality, classify rollout configurations for the empirical mismatch budget in 3.2, and calibrate the admission check in 3.3. Held-out KL evaluation. We evaluate Kx(c) and (c) on 530 held-out math problems from AIME24 (MAA, 2024) and MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024). At each evaluation checkpoint, responses are generated by the standard BF16 engine; the student and teacher score the same tokens. We compare each configuration with the standard run at the same training step. As defined in Eq. (3), (c) is the relative change in mean held-out KL; the bootstrap interval resamples problems. Primary quality rule. We set the quality threshold to τ = 0.20, well above the observed run-to-run variation of at most 1.5% in final held-out KL (5.1). For scale, standard training on the 7B student reduces mean held-out KL from 0.0965 to 0.0481; 20% increase in the final value would undo about one fifth of this gain. configuration fails if (c) τ and the 95% problem-paired bootstrap interval for its KL gap from the standard run excludes zero. The rule was fixed before the runs it evaluates (App. B). Secondary accuracy rule. Accuracy is secondary because OPD optimizes teacher agreement rather than this accuracy measure directly. run fails this rule if accuracy drops by at least five percentage points and the 95% interval for the difference excludes zero. Typical intervals are about 2 points wide. Only the primary quality rule determines Bemp(τ ). Admission-check settings. Routing replay similarly aligns expert choices in mixture-ofexperts models (Ma et al., 2026). Such approaches address execution-induced mismatch, whereas quantizing only the rollout engine or using stale weights introduces mismatch by design. Rather than requiring exact agreement, this study measures how much mismatch OPD can tolerate. Correcting the update in RL. RL systems mitigate mismatch through importance weighting (Yao et al., 2025a;b; Yu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026), token or response masking (Liu et al., 2025a; Luo et al., 2026; Ling Team et al., 2025; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), and score centering, which removes mismatch-induced drift (Marek & Ryabinin, 2026b) (App. B.1). Other approaches penalize policy divergence (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026), while prior work identifies limits of per-token corrections on long responses (Li et al., 2025a). Production OPD pipelines also adopt RL-style corrections (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; NVIDIA et al., 2026). In tested OPD runs, neither truncated importance sampling nor score centering helps; under weight noise, per-token corrections cannot address prefix shifts (Section 6). Distillation on stale or fixed rollouts. Near-Policy, AsyncOPD, and -OPD study OPD with stale rollouts (Rang et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a): AsyncOPD examines KL objectives, while -OPD regulates stalesample influence. Semi-OPD and Lightning OPD instead reuse rollouts sampled once from the initial student (Zhao et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). Low-bit OPD distills quantized student (Chen et al., 2026b), whereas here the student remains in BF16 and only the rollout engine is quantized. Complementing these methods, this study measures OPDs tolerance across mismatch sources and uses calibrated budget to screen rollout configurations before training.

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: This paper examined the trade-off between rollout efficiency and training quality under traininginference mismatch in OPD. OPD tolerates mismatch that destabilizes RL, but safe ranges depend on the model and cannot be inferred from bit width or staleness alone. On the 7B student, OPD keeps its training quality up to more than 200 times standard engines mismatch, while two RL methods break at about 12 and 60 times. Under weight noise, part of OPDs error comes from the partial responses the engine reaches, prefix shift that per-token corrections cannot fix. Calibrated budgets and an admission check help select FP8 and asynchronous configurations that preserve quality, increasing KV-cache capacity and reaching the same held-out KL target 1.62 times sooner than synchronous BF16 training. sections.content: A 100-step pilot on our 7B student with emulated quantization preceded this study; its results are not reported. Its eight quantized engines trained at mismatches up to 1.47 times their offline estimates, which the admission checks margin of 1.5 covers (Section 4.3). sections.content: We study reverse-KL OPD with the single-sample estimator of Eq. (1), on math. One run per configuration. Intervals resample problems, not runs, so verdicts are provisional; repeated configurations differ by 1.0% and 1.5% in held-out KL (App. B.5). The second runs at 0.097 and 0.39, and most likely the FP8 run with weights up to 4 versions old, used newer GPU driver without control run, so that runs speed ratios include any driver difference (App. G). One main pair. The budget, 0.184 to 0.39 nats/token, is our 7B students, and no run lies inside it. Our teacher is an RL fine-tune of the student; pair farther apart may have smaller budget. The 1.5B students budget is not located, one Llama-3.2-3B run detects only held-out KL rises of 14 to 20% or more, and no training result covers Qwen3, whose 4B student failed our check that plain OPD trains on it. Length, hardware and speed. Runs last at most 200 steps on GH200 GPUs; the noise level whose verdict changed between steps 100 and 200 moved toward failure in both runs. NVFP4 is emulated (quality only). Each FP8 speed gain comes from one short run, and the memory savings credit, 5.7%, just passes its 5% bar. Time to quality and admission.
